q: In some nineteenth-century school buildings, what traveled through tubes to advance the classroom clocks together?
d: A central clock sent an air pulse once a minute. Each connected dial moved in step, keeping separate rooms on the same schedule.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History · Wall Clock
evidence: Museum describes Hahl pneumatic classroom clocks at Jefferson Junior High, master clock sending an air pulse every minute through tubes.

q: A museum’s pair of tiny shoes was found hidden inside a Yorkshire chimney breast. What purpose does the museum associate with such concealed footwear?
d: Shoes were deliberately hidden in parts of buildings. The museum interprets the practice as a protective charm, while the details of any accompanying ritual remain uncertain.
s: Museum of Witchcraft and Magic · Pair of Child’s Shoes
choices: A warning that the chimney was blocked
A marker for the chimney sweep’s next visit
A concealed payment for the builder
evidence: Holding museum catalog and donor account identify child shoes in chimney cavity; museum interprets concealed shoes as protection charms and ritual as possibility.

q: Hayward’s nineteenth-century decorative glass bulbs were meant to be thrown during a household emergency. What were they supposed to do when they shattered?
d: The sealed bulbs held a fire-suppressing liquid. Sold as fire grenades, they were an early alternative to buckets and later household extinguishers.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History · Fire Prevention Week
evidence: Museum history describes sealed decorative glass liquid-filled bulbs thrown at fires, shattering and releasing contents; identifies Hayward19centuryexample.
